claim: Alterations in the function of K+ channels such as BKCa reportedly promote breast cancer development and progression.
source: Alterations in the function of K+ channels such as the voltage- and Ca2+-activated K+ channel of large conductance (BKCa) reportedly promote breast cancer (BC) development and progression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing literature as indicated by the word 'reportedly'.

claim: BKCa splice variant is localized to the inner mitochondrial membrane of murine and human BC cells (mitoBKCa).
source: Here, we provide electrophysiological evidence for a BKCa splice variant localized to the inner mitochondrial membrane of murine and human BC cells (mitoBKCa).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: mitoBKCa modulates overall cellular and mitochondrial energy production.
source: Through a combination of genetic knockdown and knockout along with a cell permeable BKCa channel blocker, we show that mitoBKCa modulates overall cellular and mitochondrial energy production
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using genetic and pharmacological approaches.

claim: mitoBKCa mediates the metabolic rewiring referred to as the 'Warburg effect'.
source: Through a combination of genetic knockdown and knockout along with a cell permeable BKCa channel blocker, we show that mitoBKCa modulates overall cellular and mitochondrial energy production, and mediates the metabolic rewiring referred to as the 'Warburg effect'
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic and pharmacological manipulations.

claim: mitoBKCa promotes BC cell proliferation in the presence and absence of oxygen.
source: Through a combination of genetic knockdown and knockout along with a cell permeable BKCa channel blocker, we show that mitoBKCa modulates overall cellular and mitochondrial energy production, and mediates the metabolic rewiring referred to as the 'Warburg effect', thereby promoting BC cell proliferation in the presence and absence of oxygen.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing proliferation under different oxygen conditions.

claim: mitoBKCa and BKCa transcripts are detected in low or high abundance, respectively, in clinical BC specimens.
source: Additionally, we detect mitoBKCa and BKCa transcripts in low or high abundance, respectively, in clinical BC specimens.
evidence: This claim is supported by nanostring-based mRNA expression analysis of patient samples.

claim: Targeting mitoBKCa could represent a treatment strategy for selected BC patients in future.
source: Together, our results emphasize, that targeting mitoBKCa could represent a treatment strategy for selected BC patients in future.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Cancer is one of the leading causes of death worldwide, with millions of new cases diagnosed each year.
source: It is one of the leading causes of death worldwide, with millions of new cases diagnosed each year (Sung et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Breast cancer is the most prevalent form of cancer globally.
source: Globally, the most prevalent form of cancer represents breast cancer (BC; Sung et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cancer cells frequently escape from existing therapies due to adaptations.
source: Despite many available anti-cancer treatments which largely depend on the steroid and epidermal growth factor (HER2) receptor status (Dunnwald et al., 2007), cancer cells frequently escape from existing therapies due to adaptions (Wu et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Ion channels have emerged as new cancer targets.
source: Important factors that emerged as new cancer targets are ion channels (Li and Xiong, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Alterations in the expression levels and function of potassium ion (K+) channels are critically related to cancer malignancy and progression.
source: Especially alterations in the expression levels and function of potassium ion (K+) channels are critically related to cancer malignancy and progression (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: BKCa channels localize in the plasma membrane of cells and contribute to the regulation of cytosolic K+ content, plasma membrane potential, cell cycle, cell motility, and regulatory volume changes.
source: Canonical BKCa channels usually localize in the plasma membrane (PM) of cells, and contribute to the regulation of the cytosolic K+ content, the PM potential (ΔΨPM), cell cycle, and cell motility, as well as regulatory volume, changes (Burgstaller et al., 2022a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Opening of BKCa channels results in K+ efflux, increasing the electrochemical driving force for Ca2+ entry into the cancer cell and affecting pathological cell growth and survival.
source: Opening of BKCa channels results in K+ efflux, increasing the electrochemical driving force for Ca2+ entry into the cancer cell and affecting pathological cell growth and survival (Ouadid-Ahidouch and Ahidouch, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In BC cells, an upregulation of BKCa has been associated with increased malignancy.
source: Accordingly, in BC cells (BCCs), an upregulation of BKCa has been associated with increased malignancy (Huang and Jan, 2014; Mohr et al., 2022; Oeggerli et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Several K+ channels, including BKCa, have been identified in the inner mitochondrial membrane (mitoBKCa).
source: However, besides their localization in the PM, several K+ channels, including BKCa, have also been identified in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM; mitoBKCa), a topic which has been extensively reviewed recently (Checchetto et al., 2021; Kulawiak and Szewczyk, 2022; Szabo and Szewczyk, 2023; Szewczyk et al., 2009; Wrzosek et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: MitoBKCa was first described by Siemen et al. in a human glioma cell line more than 20 years ago.
source: MitoBKCa was first described by Siemen et al. in a human glioma cell line more than 20 years ago Siemen et al., 1999.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: mitoBKCa has been found in bronchial epithelial cells, neurons, skeletal muscle cells, and cardiac myocytes.
source: So far, mitoBKCa has further been found for example in bronchial epithelial cells (Dabrowska et al., 2022), neurons (Douglas et al., 2006), skeletal muscle cells (Skalska et al., 2008), and in cardiac myocytes (Xu et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In cardiac myocytes, the BKCa-DEC isoform containing a unique C-terminal exon of 50 amino acids forms the functional mitoBKCa channel at the IMM.
source: In the latter, a splice variant, the BKCa-DEC isoform containing a unique C-terminal exon of 50 amino acids, forms the functional mitoBKCa channel at the IMM (Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Little is known about the molecular identity of mitoBKCa in other cell types.
source: Little, however, is known about the molecular identity of mitoBKCa in other cell types, and mitochondrial localization of BKCa in BCCs has not been demonstrated so far.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of prior studies, as indicated by the statement.

claim: Mitochondrial localization of BKCa in BCCs has not been demonstrated so far.
source: Little, however, is known about the molecular identity of mitoBKCa in other cell types, and mitochondrial localization of BKCa in BCCs has not been demonstrated so far.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of prior studies, as indicated by the statement.

claim: Cancer cells show increased energy demands due to their high proliferation rates.
source: Cancer cells show increased energy demands due to their high proliferation rates.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cancer cell metabolism.

claim: Tumor cells compensate for their elevated energy demand by increasing metabolic activities and adapting to nutrient-poor metabolic niches in the tumor microenvironment.
source: Thus, tumor cells compensate for their elevated energy demand by increasing metabolic activities and adapting to nutrient-poor metabolic niches in the tumor microenvironment, allowing them to overcome oxygen (O2)-dependent mitochondrial metabolism (Eales et al., 2016; Gross et al., 2022; Jang et al., 2013; Nazemi and Rainero, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The metabolic switch from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis is referred to as the 'Warburg effect'.
source: This metabolic switch from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis, frequently referred to as the 'Warburg effect', describes the phenomenon that cancer cells rather secrete lactate to the extracellular matrix (ECM), instead of utilizing pyruvate to fuel the TCA cycle (Warburg, 1924).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Lactate secretion towards the ECM promotes multiple microenvironmental cues eventually causing tumor progression.
source: This lactate secretion towards the ECM was shown to promote multiple microenvironmental cues eventually causing tumor progression (de la Cruz-López et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Extracellular K+ may impair effector T-cell function and the anti-tumor immune response.
source: Interestingly, extracellular K+ may also impair effector T-cell function, and, thus, the anti-tumor immune response (Eil et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Within the cancer cell, functions of several glycolytic enzymes rely on K+.
source: while, within the cancer cell, functions of several glycolytic enzymes rely on K+ (Bischof et al., 2021; Gohara and Di Cera, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The presence of mitoBKCa contributes to K+ entry into the mitochondrial matrix to interfere with mitochondrial volume changes and the mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Further, the presence of mitoBKCa contributes to the K+ entry into the mitochondrial matrix to interfere with mitochondrial volume changes and the mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨmito) (Krabbendam et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Depolarizing stimuli induced K+ outward currents that were larger in MMTV-PyMT WT compared to BK-KO cells.
source: Patch-clamp experiments revealed, that depolarizing stimuli delivered in 20 mV increments induced K+ outward currents that were larger in MMTV-PyMT WT compared to BK-KO cells (Figure 1A and B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B ).
evidence: This claim is supported by patch-clamp experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Peak currents were drastically reduced in MMTV-PyMT WT cells upon treatment with paxilline or iberiotoxin.
source: While the current remained unaffected by these treatments in MMTV-PyMT BK-KO cells (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), peak currents (Imax) were drastically reduced in MMTV-PyMT WT cells (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by patch-clamp experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The ΔΨPM was more polarized in MMTV-PyMT WT compared to BK-KO cells.
source: The ΔΨPM was more polarized in MMTV-PyMT WT compared to BK-KO cells (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), as expected, due to the presence of hyperpolarizing BKCa channels in WT cells (N'Gouemo, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data and citation to published literature.

claim: Current-clamp experiments unveiled a basal ΔΨPM of –46.4±2.5 mV and –32.2±2.1 mV for MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells, respectively.
source: Current-clamp experiments unveiled a basal ΔΨPM of –46.4±2.5 mV and –32.2±2.1 mV for MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Iberiotoxin treatment equalized the ΔΨPM of MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells.
source: Iberiotoxin treatment equalized the ΔΨPM of the two genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Cytosolic K+ concentrations were reduced in MMTV-PyMT WT cells under basal conditions (83.1±5.8 mM for WT ctrl vs. 121.2±7.1 mM for BK-KO ctrl).
source: In line with these findings, using a recently developed, genetically encoded K+ sensor, NES lc-LysM GEPII 1.0 (Bischof et al., 2017), we found reduced cytosolic K+ concentrations ([K+]cyto) in MMTV-PyMT WT cells under basal conditions (83.1±5.8 mM for WT ctrl vs. 121.2±7.1 mM for BK-KO ctrl)
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data using a genetically encoded K+ sensor.

claim: Iberiotoxin treatment increased cytosolic K+ concentrations in MMTV-PyMT WT cells to the BK-KO cell level (109.8±10.8 mM for WT +IBTX vs. 114.6±9.8 mM for BK-KO +IBTX).
source: which increased to the BK-KO cell level in response to iberiotoxin treatment (109.8±10.8 mM for WT +IBTX vs. 114.6±9.8 mM for BK-KO +IBTX) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E)
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data using a genetically encoded K+ sensor.

claim: MDA-MB-453 cells express high levels of BKCa mRNA transcripts.
source: Subsequently, we recorded current-voltage relationships using the human BCC lines MDA-MB-453 and MCF-7, expressing either high or low levels of BKCa mRNA transcripts, respectively (Mohr et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: MCF-7 cells express low levels of BKCa mRNA transcripts.
source: Subsequently, we recorded current-voltage relationships using the human BCC lines MDA-MB-453 and MCF-7, expressing either high or low levels of BKCa mRNA transcripts, respectively (Mohr et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Analysis of the outward currents activated by depolarization demonstrated a paxilline- and iberiotoxin-sensitive current in MDA-MB-453 cells.
source: Analysis of the outward currents activated by depolarization demonstrated a paxilline- and iberiotoxin-sensitive current in MDA-MB-453 cells (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), indicative for functional BKCa channels in their PM
evidence: This claim is supported by patch-clamp experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: MCF-7 cells do not show paxilline- and iberiotoxin-sensitive currents.
source: but not in MCF-7 cells (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), which is well in line with previous studies (Mohr et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by patch-clamp experimental data shown in the figures and citation to published literature.

claim: BKCa-DECRFP showed a significantly higher overlap with the mitochondrial dye than BKCaRFP.
source: Although the mitochondrial localization score was lower for BKCa-DECRFP compared to mtRFP (compare Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H), this BKCa variant showed a significantly higher overlap with the mitochondrial dye than BKCaRFP (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in the figures.

claim: On the level of single mitochondria, the RFP signal derived from BKCa-DECRFP surrounded the MitoGREEN fluorescence signal originating from the mitochondrial matrix.
source: Despite rather moderate colocalization scores of BKCa-DECRFP with MitoGREEN, on the level of single mitochondria, the RFP signal derived from BKCa-DECRFP surrounded the MitoGREEN fluorescence signal originating from the mitochondrial matrix, as expected for a K+ channel located in the IMM (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in the figures.

claim: Both BKCaRFP and BKCa-DECRFP increased the PM outward current compared to native MCF-7 cells.
source: Compared to native MCF-7 cells (Figure 1E), both, BKCaRFP and BKCa-DECRFP, increased the PM outward current (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by patch-clamp experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Presence of BKCaRFP caused significantly bigger currents across the PM compared to BKCa-DECRFP.
source: Despite comparable expression levels of the RFP signals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L), presence of BKCaRFP caused significantly bigger currents across the PM compared to BKCa-DECRFP (Figure 1H)
evidence: This claim is supported by patch-clamp experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The conductance of both BKCaRFP and BKCa-DECRFP was sensitive to the BKCa blockers paxilline and iberiotoxin.
source: Importantly, the conductance of both channels was sensitive to the BKCa blockers paxilline and iberiotoxin, as treatment of the cells with both compounds resulted in PM conductance values comparable to those of native MCF-7 cells (Figure 1E and H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by patch-clamp experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: MMTV-PyMT WT cells exhibited significantly elevated basal [Ca2+]cyto compared to BK-KO cells under control conditions.
source: Analysis of the Fura-2 fluorescence emission ratio showed significantly elevated basal (Figure 2A) and ATP-elicited maximal [Ca2+]cyto responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) in MMTV-PyMT WT compared to BK-KO cells under control conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by Fura-2 fluorescence imaging data shown in the figures.

claim: The elevated basal [Ca2+]cyto of MMTV-PyMT WT cells was reduced to the BK-KO cell level in response to paxilline.
source: Interestingly, the elevated basal [Ca2+]cyto of WT cells was reduced to the BK-KO cell level in response to paxilline (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), but not by iberiotoxin (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by Fura-2 fluorescence imaging data shown in the figures.

claim: Iberiotoxin did not reduce the elevated basal [Ca2+]cyto of MMTV-PyMT WT cells.
source: Interestingly, the elevated basal [Ca2+]cyto of WT cells was reduced to the BK-KO cell level in response to paxilline (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), but not by iberiotoxin (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), which is a peptide-based pore-blocking toxin that cannot pass the PM (Candia et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by Fura-2 fluorescence imaging data shown in the figures and citation to published literature.

claim: Ionomycin-based calibrations confirmed the observed differences in basal [Ca2+]cyto between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells.
source: To validate the observed basal differences in [Ca2+]cyto, we additionally performed ionomycin-based calibrations by chelating intracellular Ca2+, followed by Fura-2 saturation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D - F). These experiments confirmed the observed differences in basal [Ca2+]cyto, with [Ca2+]cyto of 170.2±8.0 nM, 98.40±4.8 nM and 178.5±13.5 nM for MMTV-PyMT WT, and 102.3±4.9 nM, 96.49±3.3 nM and 114.9±4.3 nM for MMTV-PyMT BK-KO cells, under control conditions, or in the presence of paxilline or iberiotoxin, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by ionomycin-based calibration experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Both BKCa blockers reduced the basal [Ca2+]cyto in MDA-MB-453 cells.
source: Subsequently, basal and ATP-elicited maximal [Ca2+]cyto transients were recorded in the human BCC line MDA-MB-453, where both BKCa blockers reduced the basal [Ca2+]cyto (Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by Fura-2 fluorescence imaging data shown in the figure.

claim: Maximal [Ca2+]cyto in MDA-MB-453 cells was not altered by paxilline or iberiotoxin treatment.
source: while maximal [Ca2+]cyto was not altered by these treatments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Fura-2 fluorescence imaging data shown in the figure.

claim: Ionomycin-based experiments confirmed the BKCa-modulation dependent reduction of [Ca2+]cyto in MDA-MB-453 cells.
source: Again, ionomycin-based experiments confirmed the BKCa-modulation dependent reduction of [Ca2+]cyto (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H), with [Ca2+]cyto of 110.7±8.0 nM, 64.1±4.8 nM and 78.2±13.5 nM under control, paxilline- or iberiotoxin-treated conditions, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by ionomycin-based calibration experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Expression of both BKCaRFP and BKCa-DECRFP increased the maximal and basal [Ca2+]cyto in MCF-7 cells.
source: These experiments confirmed previous findings with the other BCC lines, as the expression of both splice variants increased the maximal (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1I) and basal [Ca2+]cyto (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by Fura-2 fluorescence imaging data shown in the figures.

claim: [Ca2+]cyto in MCF-7 cells was 31.5±3.7 nM, 58.1±6.4 nM and 52,9±5.6 nM in MCF-7 control cells expressing RFP, or MCF-7 cells expressing BKCaRFP or BKCa-DECRFP, respectively.
source: [Ca2+]cyto in MCF-7 cells was found to be 31.5±3.7 nM, 58.1±6.4 nM and 52,9±5.6 nM in MCF-7 control cells expressing RFP, or MCF-7 cells expressing BKCaRFP or BKCa-DECRFP, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by ionomycin-based calibration experiments.

claim: Expression of BKCa reduced [Ca2+]ER throughout all BCCs investigated.
source: Throughout all BCCs investigated, expression of BKCa reduced [Ca2+]ER, potentially indicating that the channel was (i) functional in this cell compartment and (ii) involved in regulating the Ca2+ homeostasis of the ER.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the D1ER sensor.

claim: In MMTV-PyMT WT cells, [Ca2+]ER was restored by the cell-permeable BKCa inhibitor paxilline but not by the cell-impermeable iberiotoxin.
source: In MMTV-PyMT WT cells, [Ca2+]ER was restored by the cell-permeable BKCa inhibitor paxilline (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1K) but not by the cell-impermeable iberiotoxin (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1L)
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the D1ER sensor shown in the figures.

claim: Both paxilline and iberiotoxin restored the [Ca2+]ER in MDA-MB-453 cells.
source: while both inhibitors restored the [Ca2+]ER in MDA-MB-453 cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the D1ER sensor shown in the figure.

claim: Overexpression of both RFP-tagged BKCa isoforms in MCF-7 cells depleted the [Ca2+]ER.
source: Accordingly, overexpression of both RFP-tagged BKCa isoforms in MCF-7 cells depleted the [Ca2+]ER (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the D1ER sensor shown in the figure.

claim: In MMTV-PyMT WT as well as MDA-MB-453 cells, functional expression of BKCa reduced basal [Ca2+]mito.
source: In MMTV-PyMT WT (Figure 2G) as well as MDA-MB-453 cells (Figure 2H), functional expression of BKCa reduced basal [Ca2+]mito.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the 4mtD3cpV sensor shown in the figures.

claim: In MMTV-PyMT WT and MDA-MB-453 cells, basal and maximally elicited [Ca2+]mito peaks increased in response to paxilline but not iberiotoxin treatment.
source: Interestingly, in these two BCC types, basal and maximally elicited [Ca2+]mito peaks increased in response to paxilline (Figure 2G and H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1M—P), but not iberiotoxin treatment (Figure 2G and H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1M—P).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the 4mtD3cpV sensor shown in the figures.

claim: In MCF-7 cells, basal [Ca2+]mito was only affected upon expression of the mitochondrially targeted BKCa-DECRFP, but not BKCaRFP.
source: Importantly, in MCF-7 cells, basal [Ca2+]mito was only affected upon expression of the mitochondrially targeted BKCa-DECRFP, but not BKCaRFP (Figure 2I)
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the 4mtD3cpV sensor shown in the figure.

claim: Neither BKCaRFP nor BKCa-DECRFP affected the maximal [Ca2+]mito in MCF-7 cells.
source: whereas neither of the two isoforms affected the maximal [Ca2+]mito (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the 4mtD3cpV sensor shown in the figure.

claim: ECAR measurements unveiled an increased basal ECAR of MMTV-PyMT WT compared to BK-KO cells.
source: ECAR measurements unveiled an increased basal ECAR of MMTV-PyMT WT compared to BK-KO cells (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claim: Maximal ECAR, received upon FCCP injection, was elevated in MMTV-PyMT WT compared to BK-KO cells.
source: Maximal ECAR, received upon FCCP injection, was elevated in WT compared to BK-KO cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figure.

claim: Only paxilline, but not iberiotoxin treatment equalized basal and maximal ECARs between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells.
source: Interestingly, only paxilline, but not iberiotoxin treatment equalized basal (Figure 3B) and maximal ECARs (Figure 3C) between WT and BK-KO, suggesting that intracellular BKCa channels stimulate the glycolytic activity of BCCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claim: In MDA-MB-453 cells iberiotoxin treatment did neither affect basal nor maximal ECARs.
source: Moreover, in MDA-MB-453 cells iberiotoxin treatment did neither affect basal (Figure 3D and E) nor maximal ECARs (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claim: Paxilline increased basal and maximal ECAR in MDA-MB-453 cells.
source: Contrary to MMTV-PyMT WT cells, however, paxilline increased basal and maximal ECAR in these cells (Figure 3E and F)
evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claim: MMTV-PyMT WT cells showed a higher basal and maximal OCR compared to BCCs lacking BKCa.
source: Interestingly, the increased basal and maximal ECAR (Figure 3A–C) in MMTV-PyMT WT cells correlated with a higher basal (Figure 3H) and maximal (Figure 3I) OCR compared to BCCs lacking BKCa.
evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claim: Paxilline treatment reduced the basal and maximal OCR of BKCa proficient MMTV-PyMT cells to the BK-KO level.
source: Paxilline treatment reduced the basal and maximal OCR of BKCa proficient MMTV-PyMT cells to the BK-KO level (Figure 3H and I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claim: Iberiotoxin did not affect the OCR of MMTV-PyMT WT cells.
source: while iberiotoxin did not have any effect (Figure 3H and I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claim: In MDA-MB-453 cells, paxilline treatment increased the OCR.
source: Again, in MDA-MB-453 cells, paxilline treatment had an opposite effect to the observations that were made in MMTV-PyMT WT cells, as paxilline treatment increased the OCR (Figure 3J–L)
evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claim: Iberiotoxin treatment did not affect the OCR of MDA-MB-453 cells.
source: More importantly, regardless of this difference between the BCC lines iberiotoxin treatment did consistently not affect the OCR of MDA-MB-453 cells (Figure 3J–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claim: Single time-point LC-MS measurements confirmed the metabolic differences between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells.
source: Single time-point measurements confirmed the metabolic differences between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells and further demonstrated that BKCa inhibition by paxilline directly affected the concentrations of these metabolites (Figure 3M–P).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS-based metabolomics data shown in the figures.

claim: BKCa inhibition by paxilline directly affected the concentrations of lactate, pyruvate, asparagine, and glutamine.
source: Single time-point measurements confirmed the metabolic differences between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells and further demonstrated that BKCa inhibition by paxilline directly affected the concentrations of these metabolites (Figure 3M–P).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS-based metabolomics data shown in the figures.

claim: MMTV-PyMT and MDA-MB-453 cells responded differently to paxilline treatment in terms of metabolite concentrations.
source: As observed before by the ECAR and OCR measurements, MMTV-PyMT and MDA-MB-453 cells responded, however, differently to paxilline treatment (Figure 3M–P).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS-based metabolomics data shown in the figures.

claim: TMRM measurements unveiled a less polarized ΔΨmito of MMTV-PyMT WT cells compared to BK-KO cells under control conditions.
source: These measurements unveiled a less polarized ΔΨmito of MMTV-PyMT WT cells compared to BK-KO cells under control conditions (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TMRM fluorescence imaging data shown in the figures.

claim: Paxilline, but not iberiotoxin, equalized ΔΨmito between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells.
source: Paxilline, but not iberiotoxin, equalized ΔΨmito between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TMRM fluorescence imaging data shown in the figure.

claim: Identical results regarding ΔΨmito were obtained in MDA-MB-453 cells.
source: Identical results were obtained in MDA-MB-453 cells (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TMRM fluorescence imaging data shown in the figures.

claim: ΔΨmito of MMTV-PyMT cells was tightly dependent on the extracellular glucose concentration.
source: Interestingly, we found that ΔΨmito of MMTV-PyMT cells was tightly dependent on the extracellular glucose concentration ([GLU]ex) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by TMRM fluorescence imaging data shown in the figure.

claim: Under high [GLU]ex conditions (25.0 mM), the difference in ΔΨmito between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells disappeared.
source: Under high [GLU]ex conditions (25.0 mM), the difference in ΔΨmito between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells disappeared, as ΔΨmito increased significantly in WT and decreased significantly in BK-KO cells compared to low [GLU]ex (2.0 mM) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by TMRM fluorescence imaging data shown in the figure.

claim: The [ATP]mito rundown in the presence of Oligomycin-A was identical for both BKCaRFP and BKCa-DECRFP in MCF-7 cells.

claim: MMTV-PyMT WT and MDA-MB-453 cells showed increased levels of [H2O2]mito.

claim: Iberiotoxin treatment did not affect 2-NBDG uptake in MMTV-PyMT WT cells.

evidence: This claim is supported by 2-NBDG uptake measurements shown in the figures.

claim: Paxilline treatment reduced basal accumulation of 2-NBDG in MDA-MB-453 cells.

claim: A protein band corresponding to BKCa was identified not only in whole-cell lysates, but also in isolated mitochondria.
source: A protein band corresponding to BKCa was identified not only in whole-cell lysates, but also in isolated mitochondria.

evidence: This claim is supported by MTT assay data shown in the figure.

source: These tumor- and malignancy-promoting effects were sensitive to BKCa inhibition using the cell-permeable BKCa inhibitor paxilline (Zhou and Lingle, 2014), but not the cell-impermeable blocker iberiotoxin (Candia et al., 1992), indicating that intracellular BKCa, presumably mitoBKCa, mediates malignant BCC behaviors and tumor development.

claim: Intracellular BKCa, presumably mitoBKCa, mediates malignant BCC behaviors and tumor development.
source: indicating that intracellular BKCa, presumably mitoBKCa, mediates malignant BCC behaviors and tumor development.

source: in addition to BKCa-DEC, albeit in a much smaller subset of BC.

evidence: This claim is supported by the ER Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: Subcellular Ca2+ alterations could reportedly alter cellular bioenergetics, as Ca2+ directly regulates metabolic enzymes and activities.
source: Subcellular Ca2+ alterations could reportedly alter cellular bioenergetics, as Ca2+ directly regulates metabolic enzymes and activities (Rossi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The observed alteration in sub-cellular Ca2+ homeostasis caused by BKCa, especially mitoBKCa, has severe effects on cell metabolism.
source: Indeed, extracellular flux analysis, LC-MS-based metabolomics and fluorescence-based live-cell imaging confirmed, that the observed alteration in sub-cellular Ca2+ homeostasis caused by BKCa, especially mitoBKCa, has severe effects on cell metabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by the metabolic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The presence of mitoBKCa depolarizes BCC mitochondria.
source: Our data further emphasize, that the presence of mitoBKCa, as confirmed by mitoplast patch-clamp and western blot analyses of isolated mitochondria, depolarizes BCC mitochondria, which is in line with a previous study showing an impact of mitoBKCa activation on ΔΨmito (Kicinska et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ΔΨmito imaging data and citation to published literature.

claim: mitoBKCa-dependent depolarization of ΔΨmito triggers cellular glucose dependency and reverses the activity of the mitochondrial ATP-synthase to consume ATP for restoring ΔΨmito.

evidence: This claim is based on inference from the metabolic data.

claim: BKCa-DEC-derived mitoBKCa channels promote the Warburg effect and ultimately stimulated proliferation rates of BCCs.
source: Finally, BKCa-DEC-derived mitoBKCa channels promote the Warburg effect and ultimately stimulated proliferation rates of BCCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Warburg index and proliferation data.

claim: An O2-sensitivity of mitoBKCa was observed in glioma cells, which probably increased the hypoxic resistance of these cancer cells.
source: Our data fit earlier findings from glioma cells, where an O2-sensitivity of mitoBKCa was observed, which probably increased the hypoxic resistance of these cancer cells (Gu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cardiac myocytes, under physiologic conditions, do not show a metabolic Warburg setting.
source: It is, however, important to mention, that CM, under physiologic conditions, do not show a metabolic Warburg setting, which is a common phenomenon of cancer cells propelling their O2 independency, due to the hypoxic microenvironment.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cardiac myocyte metabolism.

claim: The absence of (mito)BKCa does not alter physiologic cardiac function.
source: Moreover, it was demonstrated recently that the absence of (mito)BKCa does not alter physiologic cardiac function.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge from recent studies.

claim: Upon induction of ischemia and reperfusion injury, a lack of (mito)BKCa promoted the susceptibility of the heart to cell death, resulting in increased infarction size.
source: Only upon induction of ischemia and reperfusion injury, a lack of (mito)BKCa promoted the susceptibility of the heart to cell death, resulting in increased infarction size (Frankenreiter et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: (mito)BKCa only played a role under conditions where mitochondria are, due to the absence of O2, not properly functioning.
source: Hence, it can be concluded that (mito)BKCa only played a role under conditions where mitochondria are, due to the absence of O2, not properly functioning.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cardiac myocyte data.

claim: The results derived from cardiac myocytes are consistent with the findings in BCCs regarding (mito)BKCa function.
source: Taking this view into account, the results derived from CM are consistent with our findings in BCCs, as (mito)BKCa mediates the resistance to hypoxic stress to BCC.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparison of cardiac myocyte and BCC data.

claim: Excessive production and release of lactate leads to extracellular acidification, creating a microenvironment that promotes tumorigenesis and metastasis as well as the resistance to anti-tumor immune responses and therapy.
source: Excessive production and release of lactate, a hallmark of the Warburg effect, leads to extracellular acidification, subsequently creating a microenvironment that promotes tumorigenesis and metastasis as well as the resistance to anti-tumor immune responses and therapy (de la Cruz-López et al., 2019; Nazemi and Rainero, 2020; Wu et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Extracellular K+ accumulating within the necrotic core of solid tumors was shown to interfere with effector T-cell function triggering immune escape of cancer cells.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Live-cell imaging of extracellular metabolites in 3D BCC models should be applied in future investigations to elucidate whether mitoBKCa directly contributes to lactate-induced tumor aggressiveness or [K+]ex.
source: To elucidate whether mitoBKCa directly contributes to lactate-induced tumor aggressiveness or [K+]ex, live-cell imaging of extracellular metabolites in 3D BCC models should be applied in future investigations (Burgstaller et al., 2022b; Burgstaller et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is speculative, indicating a need for future research.

claim: BKCa-DEC transcripts are present in human BC biopsies.

evidence: This claim is supported by the nanostring data.

claim: Only a small proportion of BC patients was positive for BKCa-DEC expression.
source: Although only a small proportion of patients was positive for BKCa-DEC expression, this finding could be of considerable clinical relevance considering the link between mitoBKCa function and BCC metabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by the nanostring data.

claim: The finding of BKCa-DEC in BC biopsies could be of considerable clinical relevance considering the link between mitoBKCa function and BCC metabolism.
source: Although only a small proportion of patients was positive for BKCa-DEC expression, this finding could be of considerable clinical relevance considering the link between mitoBKCa function and BCC metabolism.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the data.

claim: The design of the study likely underestimates the incidental number of BKCa-DEC positive BC.
source: Importantly, the design of our study likely underestimates the incidental number of BKCa-DEC positive BC, as (i) only hormone-receptor positive BC specimens were included, and (ii) bulk-tumor mRNA was analyzed, hampering the detection of low-abundant or tightly regulated transcripts against a strong background of non-cancer cells present in bulk tumor tissues.
